sections.title: Is rude Japanese always rude?
sections.body: The general rule: be polite with people you don't know, and it's generally fine to relax formality once you're familiar with someone — though even among friends, a baseline of consideration is usually maintained. The real exception is close family and old friends, where dropping formality entirely isn't considered rude the way it would be with a stranger.

points.title: Using でしょうか to sound more polite
points.explanation: Attaching でしょうか to the end of a question — in place of ですか or the informal verb + か — is a quick, low-effort way to sound noticeably more polite without learning a whole new grammar system. It works after nouns, い-adjectives, な-adjectives, and verbs; with informal verb forms specifically, の is inserted directly before でしょうか.

examples.japanese: これはいくらでしょうか。
examples.english: How much is this, may I ask?

examples.japanese: あした、くるのでしょうか。
examples.english: Will you be coming tomorrow, may I ask?

points.title: The どちら word group
points.explanation: どちら is genuinely useful because it works as the polite substitute for four separate word groups at once, depending on context: どっち/こっち/そっち/あっち (which/this/that one, of two), どれ/これ/それ/あれ (which/this/that one, of three+), どこ/ここ/そこ/あそこ (where/here/there), and だれ (who — as どちらさま, an especially polite way to ask someone's identity).

examples.japanese: おてあらいはどちらでしょうか。
examples.english: Where is the restroom, may I ask? (polite for どこ)

examples.japanese: どちらさまでしょうか。
examples.english: Who may I ask is calling? (polite for だれ)

notes.title: いらっしゃる — respectful for 'to come, go, be'
notes.body: いらっしゃる is the respectful (sonkeigo) substitute for いく, くる, and いる all at once — used only to describe someone else's action, never your own. It follows the ある-verb conjugation type (see the grammar note below), not the regular いる/える pattern its spelling might suggest.

notes.title: 召し上がる — respectful for 'to eat, drink'
notes.body: 召し上がる replaces たべる and のむ when describing someone else eating or drinking. It's a regular verb for conjugation purposes.

notes.title: ご覧になる — respectful for 'to see'
notes.body: ご覧になる replaces みる, but only for someone else — you should always answer with plain みる when the question is directed at you, even if the question itself used ご覧になる.

notes.title: おっしゃる — respectful for 'to say'
notes.body: おっしゃる replaces いう. A very common set phrase built on it, おっしゃるとおりです ('it's exactly as you say'), is a polite way to agree with someone.

notes.title: なさる — respectful for 'to do, play'
notes.body: なさる replaces する, which means any noun+する verb (勉強する, 練習する, etc.) becomes noun+なさる in respectful speech.

notes.title: ござる/ございます — very polite 'to have, exist'
notes.body: ございます (from ござる, which isn't used on its own in modern speech) is a very polite replacement for ある. Unlike the other verbs in this lesson, it doesn't raise anyone up: it is polite language (丁寧語), not respectful language, so it is fine, and very common, for your own side. Shop staff say 「こちらにございます」 about their own goods.

points.title: The ある-type verb conjugation pattern
points.explanation: This lesson introduces a fifth verb category alongside the four you already know (regular, いる/える, いる/える exception, irregular): the ある-type. These verbs end in る in their dictionary form, but conjugate by changing that final る to い before attaching the usual ます-family endings — not by dropping る the way いる/える verbs do. This pattern only shows up among respectful verbs, and only a small handful exist, so it's a short list to memorize rather than a broad new rule.

examples.japanese: いらっしゃる → いらっしゃいます
examples.english: (ある-type: る → い + ます, not る dropped)

points.title: Never use respectful verbs for yourself
points.explanation: This is the single most important rule in this lesson: respectful (sonkeigo) verbs describe someone else's actions, elevating them — using one for your own action would be backwards, roughly like accidentally praising yourself with words meant to honor someone of higher status. Even when a question is asked of you using a respectful verb, answer with a plain or humble verb instead. This same substitution extends to people in your own company or group when speaking with an outsider — you treat your own side as 'yourself' collectively.

examples.english: Will you come tomorrow? — Yes, I will. (respectful いらっしゃる for the listener, humble まいる for yourself)

notes.title: What is ヶ?
notes.body: ヶ looks like a small katakana ケ, but it's actually an abbreviated form of the kanji 箇, a counter for things. You'll see more about 箇 in Book 5 — for now, just recognize ヶ on sight and always read it as か.

notes.title: What is ふりがな?
notes.body: Small hiragana printed above a kanji, showing how to read it, is called ふりがな. It's most commonly used when a kanji's reading is unusual or difficult, and it shows up constantly in manga and in books aimed at elementary school readers.

notes.title: What is おくりがな?
notes.body: The hiragana that trails after a kanji in a verb (the part that actually conjugates, like る in 食べる) is called おくりがな — distinct from ふりがな, which sits above the kanji rather than after it.

notes.title: 自分 — oneself
notes.body: There's no single English word that maps onto 自分, because it can refer to yourself or to someone else depending on context — its meaning shifts with who's actually being discussed in the sentence, not with a fixed grammatical role.

notes.title: 持つ — to hold, have, carry, own
notes.body: The thing held, carried, or owned is marked with を. Japanese word order is genuinely flexible as long as each word keeps its particle attached — moving a phrase earlier or later in the sentence for emphasis doesn't require re-marking anything, as long as the particle travels with its word.

notes.title: 足りる — to have enough, to be sufficient
notes.body: が marks the thing there's enough of, unless は is used for stress. When asking whether a specific amount is 'enough,' で marks the amount itself rather than が.

notes.title: 作る — to make, to build
notes.body: The thing being made is marked with を, the standard object-marking pattern.

notes.title: 覚えている — to recall, remember
notes.body: This specifically means recalling something you already knew, not the act of newly memorizing or learning something for the first time — the thing recalled is marked with を, though が can replace it for emphasis.

notes.title: 使う — to use
notes.body: The thing being used is marked with を, following the usual object pattern.

points.title: いまだに — even now
points.explanation: いまだに sits at the front of the phrase it modifies and, just like its English translation 'even now,' signals that something hasn't changed despite the passage of time.

examples.japanese: いまだにかれのなまえをおぼえています。
examples.romaji: Imadani kare no namae wo oboete imasu.
examples.english: Even now, I remember his name.

points.title: 必要 — necessary, needed
points.explanation: 必要 is a な-adjective, so it needs な to directly modify a noun. As an amount marker, it can optionally take が when describing a specific quantity needed, though the が isn't required.

examples.japanese: お金がいくらひつようですか。

points.title: かわいそう — pitiful, so sad, poor thing
points.explanation: かわいそう is heard constantly as a word of sympathy when someone describes something unfortunate — it functions almost like a stock reaction, similar to saying 'oh no, that's awful' in English.

examples.japanese: きのう、わたしの犬がしにました。— かわいそう！

examples.english: My dog died yesterday. — How sad!

points.title: Counters and units generally take no particle
points.explanation: This is a reminder worth repeating: counters and amounts almost never take a particle. Attach を directly to the item being counted, and leave the number/counter itself bare — never attach を to the counter.

examples.japanese: えんぴつをごほん、もっています。
examples.english: I have 5 pencils. (を on enpitsu, not on gohon)

points.title: Describing ownership with 持っている
points.explanation: Saying you 'have' or 'own' something uses 持っている (the ている form), not the plain dictionary form — because ownership is an ongoing state, the same logic behind ています you learned for other resulting-state situations. For something you used to own but no longer do, shift to 持っていた.

examples.japanese: 車をもっていますか。— はい、にだいもっています。
examples.romaji: Kuruma wo motte imasu ka. — Hai, nidai motte imasu.
examples.english: Do you own a car? — Yes, I own two.

points.title: The machine counter だい
points.explanation: だい counts computers, TVs, cars, and most other machines and electrical appliances.

examples.japanese: テレビがさんだいあります。
examples.english: There are three television sets.

points.title: The large machine / airplane counter き
points.explanation: き is reserved for genuinely large machines — airplanes being the classic example.

examples.japanese: ひこうきがにき、みえた。
examples.english: I could see two airplanes.

points.title: Saying 'only' with しか
points.explanation: しか has no single English equivalent — it means something close to 'with the exception of' or 'only,' but it must always be paired with a negative verb, which trips up a lot of learners at first (saying 'only have $1' requires the negative form of 'have,' not the positive).

examples.japanese: いちドルしかありません。
examples.english: I only have $1.00.

points.title: Saying 'no' without being rude
points.explanation: Directly refusing a request is avoided in Japanese social contexts in favor of a handful of indirect techniques: trailing off vaguely with ちょっと... (said with a slightly pained expression, universally understood as 'no'); dropping a hint beforehand ('I'm so tired today...') so the person withdraws the request themselves; giving a polite excuse even if only loosely true ('I have plans with a friend'); or, when needed, stating an actual concrete reason. The common thread is avoiding a flat 'no' — Japanese social norms treat directness here as something to soften, not something to state bluntly.

notes.title: あげる — to give
notes.body: The receiver of the gift is marked with に; the item given is marked with を. Many learners find it worth checking sentence structure against this pattern directly — say who's giving what to whom, in that order, and the particles fall into place.

notes.title: 落ちる — to fall down, drop
notes.body: The item that falls is marked with が; the place it falls from is marked with から.

points.title: Common mistake: verbs for wearing things
points.explanation: Unlike English, which uses one all-purpose verb ('to wear') for any clothing, Japanese picks a different verb depending on where on the body the item goes. Using the wrong one is one of the clearest markers of a non-native speaker, so it's worth locking these down early rather than defaulting to one verb for everything.

examples.english: I put on a hat. (かぶる — head)

points.title: 着る — to wear (shirts, jackets)
points.explanation: The clothing worn is marked with を. 着る covers clothing worn above the waist and below the neck.

examples.japanese: さむいから、ジャケットをきます。
examples.english: I will wear a jacket because it is cold.

examples.japanese: ドレスをぜんぜんきません。

points.title: はく — to wear (shoes, pants)
points.explanation: The clothing worn is marked with を. はく is used for almost anything worn below the waist.

examples.english: You are wearing new shoes, aren't you?

examples.japanese: きのう、くろいスカートをはきました。
examples.english: I wore a black skirt yesterday.

points.title: かぶる — to wear or put on (hats)
points.explanation: かぶる is used almost exclusively for things worn on top of the head; glasses use a separate verb, かける, instead.

examples.japanese: 外はあついから、ぼうしをかぶります。
examples.romaji: Soto wa atsui kara, boushi wo kaburimasu.
examples.english: It is hot outside, so I will wear a hat.

points.title: Modifying a noun with a verb
points.explanation: This lesson introduces using a verb (or verb phrase) to describe a noun the same way an adjective would — the informal form of the verb goes directly in front of the noun it modifies, with no particle in between. This works exactly like the い-adjective modification you already know, just with a verb standing in the adjective's slot.

examples.japanese: わたしがかったかばん
examples.english: the bag I bought

examples.japanese: きのうみたえいが
examples.english: the movie I watched yesterday

points.title: It appears to be — the そう adjective ending
points.explanation: Dropping an い-adjective's final い and adding そう makes 'it appears/seems [adjective]' — a guess based on appearance rather than a confirmed fact.

examples.japanese: このケーキはおいしそうです。
examples.english: This cake looks delicious.

examples.japanese: あの人はいそがしそうです。
examples.english: That person looks busy.

points.title: It DOESN'T appear to be — the なさそう ending
points.explanation: For the negative version, first conjugate the adjective into its negative form, drop the trailing ない down to な, and add さそう.

examples.japanese: きょうはさむくなさそうです。
examples.english: It doesn't seem cold today.

examples.japanese: この本はおもしろくなさそうです。
examples.english: This book doesn't look interesting.

points.title: な-adjectives with そう and なさそう endings
points.explanation: な-adjectives take そう and なさそう the same way, but attach directly rather than needing an い dropped first.

examples.japanese: あのこうえんはしずかそうです。
examples.romaji: Ano kouen wa shizuka sou desu.
examples.english: That park looks quiet.

examples.japanese: ホテルのへやはきれいじゃなさそうです。
examples.romaji: Hoteru no heya wa kirei janasasou desu.
examples.english: The hotel room doesn't seem clean.

points.title: Making a そう phrase modify a noun with な
points.explanation: To use a そう/なさそう phrase directly in front of a noun (rather than as a standalone sentence ending in です), attach な between そう and the noun — the same な-adjective attachment rule you already know.

sections.title: The bonus system
sections.body: Many Japanese companies pay full-time workers a bonus twice a year, usually in June and December, ranging from 1.5 to 3 times a month's salary depending on individual and company performance. It's common to see this money go toward major purchases — a car, a family trip — and some retailers even let customers defer payment until after bonus season.

notes.title: 出る — to appear, come out
notes.body: が marks the thing appearing or coming out. The place something leaves from can instead be marked with から (from) or を (object marker), depending on framing.

notes.title: 知る — to know
notes.body: を marks the thing known. Because knowing something is an ongoing state, asking or stating that you know something always uses the ~ています form — 知ります or 知りません are simply not correct here, the way they might seem to be by analogy with other verbs.

notes.title: 運転する — to drive
notes.body: を marks the vehicle being driven. To ask whether someone is able to drive, できる combines with を on the vehicle, following the same object-marking rule.

notes.title: 乗る — to ride, get on, get in
notes.body: に marks the vehicle being ridden or gotten into — cars, rides, airplanes, anything you get onto or into.

points.title: こと meaning 'about'
points.explanation: こと is genuinely versatile — thing, matter, fact, circumstance, reason, experience — more meanings than will fit in your head at once, so this lesson introduces it piece by piece. Its most basic use is 'about': attach こと after a noun with の to talk about that topic.

examples.japanese: しごとのこと
examples.english: about work

points.title: こと with adjectives means 'thing'

points.title: A less obvious use of こと
points.explanation: Saying 'I like you' most simply is あなたが好きです, but 'I like about you' — あなたのことが好きです — is just as common in practice, even though it looks odd translated literally. こと also pairs naturally with question words: だれのことですか asks 'who are you talking about?'

examples.english: When are you talking about?

points.title: Have you ever...?
points.explanation: Combining an informal PAST-tense verb with ことがありますか asks whether someone has ever had a certain experience. It's critical not to shift the tense of the verb directly before こと — doing so changes the meaning significantly, since the whole point of this pattern relies on the verb staying in its informal past form.

examples.japanese: みそしるをのんだことがありますか。

examples.english: Have you ever drunk miso soup?

examples.romaji: Roshia ni itta koto ga arimasu ka.
examples.english: Have you ever been to Russia?

points.title: 'I have...' and 'I have never...'
points.explanation: The tense of ある in this pattern shifts to state whether the experience has happened or not — ことがあります for 'I have,' ことがありません for 'I have never.' ない is a more casual version of ありません.

examples.japanese: 日本のえいがをみたことがありません。
examples.romaji: Nihon no eiga wo mita koto ga arimasen.
examples.english: I have never seen a Japanese movie.

examples.japanese: がいこくにいったことがない。
examples.romaji: Gaikoku ni itta koto ga nai.
examples.english: I have never been to a foreign country. (casual)

points.title: The これほど word group
points.explanation: これほど、それほど、あれほど、どれほど follow the same familiar kore/sore/are/dore pattern first seen in Book 1, meaning 'this much,' 'that much,' 'to that extent,' and '(no matter) how much,' with the same closeness-based logic determining which one fits.

examples.japanese: なんでそれほどパンをかいましたか。
examples.romaji: Nande sorehodo pan wo kaimashita ka.
examples.english: Why did you buy so much bread?

points.title: Looking forward to something
points.explanation: 楽しみにしています expresses looking forward to something, with を marking the thing anticipated. It can also combine with a こと-nominalized verb phrase to look forward to an event or action, and can shorten to 楽しみ or お楽しみ standing alone as a noun meaning 'something to look forward to' — in that shortened noun form, は or が replaces を.

notes.title: 出張する — to take a business trip
notes.body: The destination of the business trip is marked with に, the standard location-marking pattern.

examples.japanese: らいしゅう、おおさかにしゅっちょうします。
examples.english: I'm going on a business trip to Osaka next week.

points.title: Which particle goes with 曲がる (to turn)
points.explanation: 曲がる's particle depends on what you're describing. The direction you turn takes に or へ: 右に曲がる and 右へ曲がる both mean "turn right" (に is more common in everyday speech). The corner or road you go around takes を: 角を曲がる, "turn the corner". The place where you make the turn takes で: 信号で曲がる, "turn at the stoplight".

examples.japanese: 右にまがってください。
examples.english: Turn right please.

examples.japanese: あのしんごうでまがりました。
examples.english: I turned at that stoplight.

points.title: 上がる — to go or come up
points.explanation: When going up along or through something (stairs, a slope), the thing is marked with を. When going up to a destination (a floor, a rooftop), the destination is marked with に.

examples.japanese: かいだんをあがりましょう。
examples.english: Let's go up the stairs.

examples.japanese: おくじょうにあがってください。
examples.english: Please go up to the rooftop.

points.title: 降りる — to go down, get off
points.explanation: 降りる covers coming down off of something (a mountain, a platform) and getting off a vehicle (a car, a plane, an elevator). から marks what's being gotten off of when emphasizing the starting point; を marks it when emphasizing the act of leaving it.

examples.japanese: エレベーターでおります。
examples.english: I will go down by elevator.

examples.japanese: 車からおりました。
examples.english: I got out of the car.

points.title: The special case: まっすぐ never takes に
points.explanation: While に (or へ) attaches to 右 and 左 to mark direction, まっすぐ (straight ahead) never takes a particle — the same way English says 'turn to the right' but never 'go to straight ahead.' The exception makes sense once you notice English follows the identical pattern.

examples.japanese: まっすぐいってください。
examples.english: Please go straight ahead. (no に)

examples.japanese: 右にまがってください。
examples.english: Please turn to the right. (contrast: に is needed here)

points.title: Asking how something is done with どうやって
points.explanation: どうやって, followed by a verb phrase, asks 'how do you [verb]?' — asking about the method or manner of doing something.

examples.japanese: それをどうやってたべますか。— フォークでたべます。
examples.romaji: Sore wo dou yatte tabemasu ka. — Fooku de tabemasu.
examples.english: How do you eat that? — You eat it with a fork.

points.title: Demonstrating how something was done
points.explanation: Answering a どうやって question can use そうやって, ああやって, or こうやって, depending on distance/closeness — the same ko/so/a logic as every other word group in this family. こうやって is used when you're the one physically demonstrating the action or holding up the example; そうやって or ああやって refer to an action done by someone else or further away.

examples.japanese: こうやってたべます。
examples.english: I eat it like this. (demonstrating yourself)

examples.japanese: そうやってきっぷをかいます。
examples.english: You buy tickets like that.

points.title: Counting floors

examples.english: It's on the 1st floor.

examples.japanese: さんがいにあります。
examples.english: It's on the 3rd floor. (irregular さんがい, not さんかい)

sections.title: Getting around by train
sections.body: Japan's major cities run on train and subway systems extensive enough that owning a car often isn't necessary — trains are famously clean, frequent, and close to always on time (delays are rare enough that a late train is genuinely notable). Prepaid IC cards, tapped directly on station turnstiles, replace buying a paper ticket for every single ride, and the same card typically works at convenience stores and vending machines too.

points.title: Asking for permission with てform + いいですか
points.explanation: Attaching いいですか to any verb's て-form asks 'is it all right if I [verb]?' — one of the most common permission-asking patterns in everyday Japanese.

examples.japanese: これをたべてもいいですか。
examples.romaji: Kore wo tabete mo iidesu ka.
examples.english: Is it all right if I eat this?

examples.japanese: よんじにかえってもいいですか。
examples.romaji: Yonji ni kaette mo iidesu ka.
examples.english: Is it okay if I return home at 4 o'clock?

points.title: Answering yes to a permission question
points.explanation: Answer with the same て-form + いいです pattern used to ask, meaning 'it's okay if you do.' You may hear よ tacked onto the end in casual speech, and it's also completely normal to answer with just いいです or いいですよ on their own, without repeating the verb.

examples.japanese: たべてもいいです。
examples.english: It's okay if you eat it.

points.title: Answering no — and why directness is avoided
points.explanation: Simply answering だめ ('no good') to a permission question is grammatically valid but comes across as unusually blunt in Japanese social norms — reserved mainly for speaking to your own young children, and even then it would feel strange to use it toward someone else's child. The standard, polite way to decline is the て-form followed by はだめです ('it's not all right if you [verb]').

examples.japanese: これをのんではだめです。
examples.romaji: Kore wo nonde wa dame desu.
examples.english: No, it's not all right if you drink it.

examples.japanese: いいえ、それはわたしのです。
examples.romaji: Iie, sore wa watashi no desu.
examples.english: No, that is mine. (a softer indirect refusal)

points.title: Informal versions of asking and answering permission
points.explanation: Even in business settings, once people know each other, formality often relaxes. Informally, いいですか shortens to いい?, and the response shortens correspondingly — casual speech is genuinely common in Japan, not reserved only for close friends the way textbooks sometimes imply.

examples.japanese: これ、たべていい？— うん、いいよ。
examples.romaji: Kore, tabete ii? — Un, ii yo.
examples.english: Can I eat this? — Yeah, sure. (casual versions of いいですか / はい、いいです)

points.title: が vs けど — both mean 'but'
points.explanation: が and けど both connect two contrasting sentences, but they pair with different formality levels: が sits most naturally after a polite (です/ます) sentence, while けど feels more natural following an informal sentence. Choosing consistently matched formality on both sides of the connector is part of what makes a sentence sound native rather than just grammatically correct.

sections.title: Company trips and graduation trips
sections.body: JTB (Japan Travel Bureau) is Japan's largest travel agency and one of the largest in the world. Many Japanese companies fund a domestic or international trip for employees once or twice a year as a perk, and it's common for college and even some high school students to take a celebratory trip right after graduating. Newlyweds also frequently travel abroad specifically for their honeymoon.

notes.title: 凄い modifying a word — な or の, both heard
notes.body: 凄い is technically a な-adjective, but you'll hear both 凄いな and 凄いの used when it directly modifies a following word — searching either version online turns up plenty of real examples, so don't be surprised to see both in the wild.

points.title: 辞める — to quit one's job (or a club/responsibility)
points.explanation: The thing quit is marked with を. 辞める is specifically for stepping away from an ongoing role or membership — a job, a club, an instrument you were learning.

points.title: 止める — to stop, to quit (a habit or plan)
points.explanation: The thing being ended is marked with を. 止める is used for stopping a plan, quitting a habit like smoking, or ending something in progress — a different scope from 辞める's job/membership focus, even though both are translated 'to quit' in English.

examples.english: I quit smoking.

examples.japanese: どうやってしゃっくりをやめますか。

examples.english: How do you stop the hiccups?

points.title: 決める — to decide, to choose (active)
points.explanation: This lesson introduces the first active/passive verb pair in this series: 決める describes YOU or someone actively making a decision. The item being decided is marked with を; the item ultimately selected is marked with に.

examples.japanese: これにきめました。
examples.english: I decided on this.

examples.japanese: ドレスをきめたいです。
examples.english: I want to choose a dress.

examples.japanese: どの車にきめましたか。
examples.english: Which car did you decide on?

points.title: 決まる — to be decided, settled (passive)
points.explanation: 決まる differs sharply from 決める: it describes a decision that wasn't actively made by any one specific person — typically something settled by a committee or group the speaker wasn't directly part of. Notice the particle also shifts: the item decided is marked with が, not を.

points.title: 生きる — to be alive
points.explanation: The most common form of this verb is 生きています, meaning 'I am alive,' or, as a question, 生きていますか, asking whether someone is still alive.

examples.japanese: あなたのおとうさんはまだいきていますか。
examples.romaji: Anata no otousan wa mada ikite imasu ka.
examples.english: Is your father still alive?

examples.japanese: アインシュタインはもういきていません。
examples.english: Einstein is no longer living.

points.title: 死ぬ — to die
points.explanation: More formal alternatives to 死ぬ exist (なくなる is one), but 死ぬ is extremely common in everyday speech, and it isn't limited to people — it's also used casually for pets and even for electronics or cars that have stopped working. Because death is treated as an ongoing state once it happens, saying someone has died uses the ~ています form (死んでいます, 'is dead'), not the plain past tense.

examples.japanese: きんぎょがしにました。
examples.english: My goldfish died.

examples.romaji: Hayaku shinitakunai node, mainichi ekusasaizu wo shite imasu.
examples.english: Since I don't want to die early, I exercise every day.

points.title: Choosing with にする
points.explanation: する combined with に is a second way to say something is chosen over another option — distinct from 決める, which can also mean 'I decided,' something にする alone cannot express. する paired with any other particle changes its meaning entirely, so this combination is specifically tied to choosing.

examples.romaji: Nani ni shimasu ka. — Orenji jyuusu ni shimasu.

notes.title: 勝つ (to win) and 負ける (to lose)
notes.body: Counters like money take no particle at all with these two verbs. The object particle を marks the thing won or lost when it's an event (a race, a match). で marks the means by which something was won or lost (a game, a specific method). に marks who was beaten or who someone lost to.

notes.title: 教える — to teach, to tell
notes.body: 教える is used constantly to mean 'to tell,' not just formal teaching — a common everyday phrase, 名前を教えてください, literally means 'teach me your name' but is simply how Japanese asks someone their name politely. The thing taught or told is marked with を.

notes.title: 捨てる — to throw away
notes.body: The item being thrown away is marked with を, the standard object-marking pattern.

notes.title: 迷う — to get lost, to be perplexed, to hesitate
notes.body: The thing being hesitated over is marked with を. This verb is genuinely useful when you're torn between two options — if a friend asks which of two items you'll choose and you haven't decided, 迷っています ('I'm undecided') is a natural, very common response.

points.title: びっくりする — to be surprised (and marking the reason)
points.explanation: This pattern for marking the reason behind being surprised isn't limited to びっくりする — it extends to plenty of other verbs and verb phrases too. で marks the reason when it's a な-adjective or a noun. When the reason is an い-adjective, that adjective conjugates into its くて form instead, and the tense of the whole statement is carried by the final verb, not the adjective. い-adjectives have a second option too: adding ので directly after the plain adjective works just as well as the くて form — while な-adjectives and nouns need だ (or です) inserted before ので.

examples.japanese: かれのりょうりがおいしくて、びっくりしました。
examples.romaji: Kare no ryouri ga oishikute, bikkuri shimashita.
examples.english: I was surprised that his cooking was delicious.

examples.english: I was surprised it was so cheap.

examples.japanese: ひまなので、びっくりしました。
examples.english: I was surprised it was so quiet business-wise. (な-adjective + な + ので)

points.title: The かた suffix — 'how to' or 'the way to'
points.explanation: Attaching かた to a verb creates 'how to [verb]' or 'the way to [verb].' The attachment point depends on verb type: for regular verbs, use the い-form and add かた; for いる/える verbs, drop る and add かた.

units.title: Doing Things Like X, Y, and Z

notes.title: 笑う (to laugh) and 泣く (to cry)
notes.body: Nothing unusual about these two — the reason for laughing or crying is expressed the same way you've marked reasons in every earlier lesson, with で, から, or a くて-form adjective.

notes.title: 怒る — to be mad, angry
notes.body: The person someone is mad at is marked with に. Since being mad is treated as an ongoing state, this verb is almost always used in ~ています form rather than the plain present tense.

notes.title: シャワーをあびる — to take a shower
notes.body: あびる isn't limited to showers — it's used more broadly for being showered with something, including sunlight or other things falling over your body.

notes.title: 流す — to flush, shed, wash off
notes.body: The thing being flushed or washed away is marked with を. This verb is also used somewhat poetically to mean shedding tears or, more dramatically, shedding blood.

notes.title: 首になる — to be fired
notes.body: This literally translates to 'to become a neck,' which sounds odd out of context but is simply the standard idiom for losing a job.

points.title: Combining いく and くる with other verbs
points.explanation: いく and くる can attach to another verb's い-form (for regular verbs) or dictionary-form-minus-る (for いる/える verbs) to express going or coming somewhere for a purpose — 'go to see,' 'come to eat.'

examples.english: I will go to see a movie.

examples.japanese: ともだちがあそびにきます。
examples.english: My friend is coming to hang out.

points.title: Changing the tense and form of いく／くる in this pattern
points.explanation: Once you know the basic pattern, conjugating the いく/くる half opens up a wide range of natural sentences without learning anything new.

points.title: The たり verb form
points.explanation: たり builds a representative list of actions — English does this with 'things like,' listing a few examples rather than every single thing. It's built off the informal past form (positive or negative): add り directly to it.

points.title: Building a full たり sentence
points.explanation: Any number of たり verbs can be strung together, each one conjugated into たり form, with する (in whatever tense fits) attached at the very end to close the list. The tense of the entire sentence is carried entirely by that final する — the たり verbs themselves stay fixed regardless of the sentence's overall tense.

points.title: Using the same verb twice with たり
points.explanation: Repeating the same verb in たり form (once positive, once negative) creates a 'sometimes I do, sometimes I don't' meaning — a distinct nuance from listing different verbs.

examples.japanese: あねははたらいたり、はたらかなかったりします。

points.title: Using かな — 'I wonder if'
points.explanation: Attaching かな to the end of a sentence turns it into 'I wonder if...' Historically this was considered mostly male speech, with women traditionally using かしら for the same meaning — but in modern Japan, かな is now common among young women as well. Because it has a casual, thinking-out-loud tone, it's best used carefully with people you don't know well.

examples.japanese: あした、雨がふるかな。
examples.english: I wonder if it will rain tomorrow.

notes.title: 取る and 撮る — both mean 'to take'
notes.body: 取る and 撮る are used identically, differing only in which kanji fits the situation — 撮る specifically for photos, 取る for everything else. The item taken is marked with を.

notes.title: 年を取る — to age, get old
notes.body: A very natural mistake is assuming that ふるい (old) plus its adjective-to-verb pattern would work for aging in years — it doesn't. For a living thing getting older in age, 年を取る is the correct phrase, not a conjugated form of ふるい.

notes.title: 心配する — to worry
notes.body: You already know 心配 as a description ('I am worried about ___'); attaching する turns it into a full verb. The thing worried about is marked with を.

notes.title: 説明する — to explain
notes.body: The thing being explained is marked with を, the standard object pattern.

points.title: Extending くなる to verb forms
points.explanation: The same drop-final-い-add-くなる trick works on any verb form that happens to end in い — most usefully たい (want to), たくない (don't want to), and the negative て-form. The resulting phrase carries a nuance English doesn't have a clean single-word equivalent for: it implies a change from how things were before. いきたくなりました doesn't just mean 'I wanted to go' — it means something closer to 'I didn't want to before, but now I do.'

sections.title: Regional dialects in Japan
sections.body: Standard Japanese (based largely on Tokyo speech) is what's taught in textbooks and used in national broadcasting, but regional dialects remain very much alive — Kansai-ben (from the Osaka/Kyoto area) and Touhoku-ben (northern Japan) are two of the most recognizable, with distinct vocabulary, verb endings, and pitch patterns. Many differences are subtle enough that a beginner might not notice them, but there are genuinely quite a few once you know to listen for them.

notes.title: 借りる — to borrow, to rent
notes.body: The item borrowed is marked with を — except amounts of money, which as counters take no particle at all. The person or place borrowed from is marked with either に or から; both are correct and mean the same thing.

notes.title: 貸す — to loan, to lend
notes.body: The item being lent follows the same を/no-particle-for-amounts rule as 借りる. The person receiving the loan is marked with に.

notes.title: 返す — to return, to pay back
notes.body: The item being returned is marked with を, the same object pattern as the rest of this verb family.

notes.title: 夜更かしする — to stay up late
notes.body: This is a milder cousin of 徹夜する (pulling an all-nighter, not sleeping at all) — 夜更かしする just means staying up later than usual, not skipping sleep entirely.

notes.title: 点ける — to turn on
notes.body: The item turned on is marked with を. A more mechanical-sounding alternative, especially for electronics, is 電源を入れる ('to insert the power'), commonly heard for computers and similar devices.

notes.title: 消す — to turn off, to erase
notes.body: The item turned off or erased is marked with を. The opposite mechanical phrase, 電源を切る ('to cut the power'), pairs with 電源を入れる the same way 消す pairs with 点ける.

points.title: You should — べきです
points.explanation: Attaching べきです after a verb's informal past (た) form creates 'you should [verb].' Despite using the past-tense form, the meaning has nothing to do with past tense — don't let that surface detail throw you off.

examples.japanese: まいにち、かんじをべんきょうするべきです。

points.title: You shouldn't — べきです with the ない form

examples.english: You shouldn't stay up late.

points.title: If-then statements: an overview
points.explanation: Japanese has four distinct ways to build an if-then statement, and this lesson covers the first two. Every if-then statement has a condition (the 'if' part) and a result (the 'then' part), in that order, matching English word order.

examples.japanese: 雨がふれば、いきません。
examples.english: If it rains, I won't go. (condition, then result)

examples.japanese: やすければ、かいます。
examples.english: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.

points.title: If-then with なら
points.explanation: The simplest of the four: attach なら directly after an informal sentence (dropping だ/です if the sentence would otherwise end in one) to state the condition, then follow with the result. もし at the start of the sentence is optional and simply reinforces that it's a hypothetical. The result half isn't limited to a plain statement — it can be a request, suggestion, command, or question.

examples.japanese: もし今年日本にいかないなら、らいねんいきます。
examples.romaji: Moshi kotoshi Nihon ni ikanai nara, rainen ikimasu.
examples.english: If I don't go to Japan this year, I'll go next year.

examples.japanese: このみせがやすいなら、ここでかいましょう。
examples.romaji: Kono mise ga yasui nara, koko de kaimashou.
examples.english: If this store is cheap, let's buy it here.

points.title: If-then with たら
points.explanation: Add ら to a verb's informal past (た) form to build the second if-then type.

examples.japanese: もしお金がなかったら、かします。
examples.english: If you don't have money, I will lend you some.

examples.japanese: 六時までにかえったら、すきなばんぐみをみます。
examples.romaji: Rokuji made ni kaettara, sukina bangumi wo mimasu.
examples.english: If I get home by 6 o'clock, I will watch my favorite show.

points.title: たら used to mean 'when'
points.explanation: たら is genuinely dual-purpose — context alone decides whether it means 'if' or 'when,' and often the sentence works equally well translated either way. One reliable clue: if もし opens the sentence, it's definitely an if-then statement, not a 'when' statement.

examples.japanese: しゅくだいをおわったら、テレビをみます。
examples.romaji: Shukudai wo owattara, terebi wo mimasu.
examples.english: When I finish my homework, I will watch TV.

examples.romaji: Souji wo shite itara, tomodachi ga kimashita.
examples.english: When I was cleaning, my friend came over.

points.title: Using か with verb phrases for 'whether X or Y'
points.explanation: Book 3 taught か connecting nouns to mean 'or.' The same か can connect entire verb phrases (in informal form) to ask or state 'whether X or Y' — and this isn't limited to two options; any number of informal clauses can be chained with か between them, with the very last verb setting the overall politeness of the sentence.

notes.title: 準備する — to prepare
notes.body: The thing being prepared is marked with を. This behaves identically to the already-familiar 用意する.

notes.title: 喧嘩する — to fight, have a fight
notes.body: The person being fought with is marked with と. The reason for the fight can be marked with で, ので, or a くて-form adjective — or, to say what the fight was about, のことで or について ('concerning') work as well.

notes.title: 要る — to need
notes.body: The thing needed is marked with が. Its dictionary form looks identical to いる (to be/exist, animate), but don't let the spelling fool you — this is an いる/える exception verb, conjugated as a regular verb, not the same conjugation pattern as existence-いる.

notes.title: 貯める — to save, to collect
notes.body: The thing being saved or collected is marked with を, the standard object pattern.

notes.title: 頂く — to receive (most polite)
notes.body: The item received is marked with を; the giver is marked with に or から. This is the most polite of the receiving verbs, reserved for receiving something from someone clearly above you in status.

notes.title: もらう — to receive (neutral, everyday)
notes.body: Grammatically identical to 頂く — item marked with を, giver marked with に or から — but noticeably less formal. This is the version to reach for by default with people of equal or lower status, and in most ordinary situations.

notes.title: くれる — to be given (only toward yourself)
notes.body: This is the one genuinely tricky verb in the set: くれる can ONLY be used when the thing is given TO you or your own group — never when describing a gift passing between two other people. The item is marked with を; the giver is marked with が.

notes.title: あげる — to give (modern usage)
notes.body: Historically あげる was reserved for giving to someone of equal or higher status, but in modern Japanese it's used regardless of status difference. The item given is marked with を; the giver is marked with が; the recipient is marked with に.

notes.title: やる — to give (now largely restricted to animals/plants)
notes.body: やる used to be the standard verb for giving to someone of lower status, but that usage now reads as blunt or even rude toward a person. In modern practice it survives mainly for feeding animals or watering plants — あげる has taken over nearly everywhere else.

notes.title: 手伝う — to help out
notes.body: The task or person being helped is marked with を.

points.title: Saying 'I want you to...'
points.explanation: Attach ほしい after a verb's て-form to say you want someone else to do something — a distinct pattern from たい, which is about your own wants. The person you want to do the action is marked with に, but it's routinely dropped when it's obvious from context — if you're speaking directly to the person, naming them again would sound unnaturally formal.

notes.title: 壊す — to break (something), active
notes.body: The thing broken is marked with を. This verb can also describe your own body breaking down — 体を壊しました means 'I got sick,' not literally breaking a body part.

notes.title: 壊れる — to be broken, passive
notes.body: The thing that broke is marked with が. Since being broken is a state that persists, this is almost always used in ~ています form, the same pattern behind every other ongoing-state verb in this series.

notes.title: 生まれる — to be born
notes.body: The living thing (or, metaphorically, an idea) being born is marked with が.

points.title: The て-form combined with もらう and いただく
points.explanation: Attaching もらう or いただく after any verb's て-form creates 'to have someone do [verb] for me.' いただく is the humble version, used when the person doing the action is of higher status than you; もらう is the everyday, far more common version in modern Japanese.

examples.japanese: ともだちにやさいをかってもらいました。
examples.romaji: Tomodachi ni yasai wo katte moraimashita.
examples.english: I had my friend buy vegetables (for me).

examples.romaji: Sensei ni kanji wo oshiete itadakimashita.
examples.english: I had my teacher teach me kanji.

points.title: The て-form combined with くれる and あげる
points.explanation: てくれる means someone does something for you, as a favor; てあげる means you do something for someone else, as a favor. Both carry the same underlying implication as the plain giving/receiving verbs from Lesson 13: the action genuinely benefits the receiving person.

examples.japanese: あねがいつもたすけてくれます。
examples.english: My older sister always helps me out.

examples.japanese: ともだちにお金をかしてあげました。
examples.romaji: Tomodachi ni okane wo kashite agemashita.
examples.english: I lent money to my friend (as a favor).

points.title: Putting it all together — the full family of て-form patterns
points.explanation: This lesson's five patterns — てもらう, ていただく, てくれる, てあげる, and Lesson 13's てほしい — all share the same building block (a verb's て-form) but each expresses a different direction of favor: who's doing the action, and who benefits from it. Getting comfortable choosing the right one is less about memorizing a rule and more about tracking, in any given sentence, who is helping whom.

examples.english: I want you to write a letter. (てほしい — what I want from someone)

examples.japanese: いしゃにみていただきました。
examples.english: I had the doctor look at it. (ていただく — someone of higher status helps me)
